processing: Medium oxidation with firm shaking, strip-rolled and charcoal roasted medium to medium-heavy; the thick, upright leaf takes roast well, and the cultivar is also used for black tea.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May (a mid-season sprouter), as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Long, straight, tightly rolled dark strips, often with visible stem, and a sweet plum-like smell.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, elongated olive leaves with red rims and prominent veins.
taste_profile: Plum and dark fruit with a floral top note, a firm, slightly tannic body, warm roast and a long, sweet mineral finish; sturdier than the aromatic hybrid cultivars.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, gaiwan or zisha pot. It has more grip than most yancha, so keep the first three steeps short; the tannin turns to sweetness from the fourth.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. A medium-heavy roast makes it a good keeper: it drinks well after six months of rest, improves for a year or two and holds three to five years sealed and dry; it also takes re-roasting and ageing well.
description:
Mei Zhan is an old Anxi cultivar that has become one of the most useful plants in Fujian, and in the Wuyi Mountains it makes a robust, plum-scented rock tea that sits between the famous bushes and the cheap aromatic hybrids in both character and price.

The bush is an upright, large-leaved type that by tradition came from Lu Tian in Anxi county in the nineteenth century, and it travelled because it adapts well and carries strong aroma. Across Fujian it is used for Minnan oolong and for black tea, and some Jin Jun Mei style tea is said to use it, though there are no firm figures; in Wuyi it is strip-rolled and charcoal roasted like any yancha.

The name evokes plum blossom, and the cup leans that way: ripe plum and dark fruit, a floral note on top, and a firmer, more tannic body than the Tieguanyin-derived hybrids. Makers tend to give it a medium or medium-heavy roast, which suits it; the thick leaf does not go hollow, and after a few months of rest the roast and the fruit knit into something warm and sweet with a long mineral finish.

Brew it with boiling water and quick early pours, because it has more grip than a Shui Xian; from the fourth steep the tannin turns to sweetness and it coasts for several more infusions. It is a good tea with food and a good tea to drink cooled.

It is sold by the current spring harvest, mostly from plantings outside the core scenic area, which keeps it affordable, and it ages better than its price suggests, so a sealed bag put away for a year is rarely wasted. If you enjoy its sturdiness, Tie Luo Han is the next step up in weight; if you want the same cultivar in a completely different form, try a Mei Zhan black tea.
sources_note: The Anxi Lutian origin is the traditional account in Chinese cultivar literature; the claim that much Jin Jun Mei-style black tea uses Mei Zhan leaf is common trade knowledge rather than a documented statistic.
history:
Mei Zhan is an Anxi plant from Lu Tian, counted among the county's four se zhong varieties with Ben Shan, Huang Dan and Mao Xie. Its naming stories are legends. One, set around 1821, has someone surnamed Wang from Xi Ping taking the name from a couplet at Lu Tian; another, set around 1810, credits a local scholar struck by its plum-like blossoms.

The rise of Tieguanyin later left varieties like this neglected, with planted areas shrinking.

The history of the Wuyi strip-rolled version in particular is little documented.
